abstract: Most robot policies, whether trained by imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL), map observations to action values at discrete control steps and leave the continuity of physical motion to be learned implicitly. We propose ODE policy, which learns the dynamics of the action rather than the action itself. A neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) learns the vector field of the action by matching the integrated actions to the targets over short action chunks in IL and single control steps in RL. A lightweight diversity head captures multi-modal behavior by randomizing the direction of the field. At deployment, each action is integrated from the previous one, so the executed trajectory is continuous by construction. We evaluate it as a visuomotor policy, as the action head of vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), and as the actor of model-based RL against 14 baselines on unimanual, bimanual, dexterous, locomotion, and loco-manipulation tasks. In IL, against flow matching, it reaches 5.9$\times$ the success, 5.4$\times$ the generalization, and 3.9$\times$ the mode balance after one epoch, and generates actions 10.8$\times$ faster. It mostly moves more smoothly than human demonstrations. On 14 real-world tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, dexterous, and humanoid robots, it achieves the highest success rate. In RL, it further speeds up SuperMimic for humanoid motion tracking and smooths its actions. Efficient in learning, data, parameters, and execution, ODE policy offers a promising path to scaling robot learning.

sections.body: Most robot policies in imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL) output one action value per control step, so the continuity of motion has to be learned from data. The paper proposes **ODE policy**. A neural ordinary differential equation learns the vector field of the action, conditioned on the observation, and each action is integrated from the previous one over physical time. It is trained on short action chunks in IL and on single control steps in RL. After one epoch on LIBERO, it succeeds in 79.2% of episodes, against at most 43.2% for the baselines. As the action head of a vision-language-action model, it reaches 96.0% against 75.5% for its flow matching expert. The comparison covers 14 baselines under shared backbones, data, and training schedules.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Most robot policies map observations to discrete actions and leave continuity to be learned; ODE policy instead learns the action's dynamics.

sections.body: The related work groups prior methods into four areas. Dynamical movement primitives, stable dynamical systems, and neural dynamic policies fix the form of the vector field or constrain it toward an attractor, which limits each system to a few motions. Learned state dynamics, often neural ODEs, serve model-based RL or feedback controllers, while a separate controller produces the action. Diffusion and flow matching policies integrate over a generation time that has no physical meaning. Efficient IL methods reduce sampling steps or change the flow source, and SuperMimic speeds up RL with a differentiable world model. The authors say these methods keep the actor as a direct map from states to actions, and ODE policy changes that actor.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior ODE robot policies fix the vector field's form, and efficiency methods keep direct-action actors, which ODE policy changes.

sections.body: The section formalizes direct-action policies. In IL, a policy predicts a chunk of $H$ future actions per observation, and each action is still a separate value. Diffusion and flow matching policies solve a differential equation at inference, but their time variable is a generation time without physical meaning. In RL, the actor outputs one action per control step, and model-based methods backpropagate return through imagined rollouts. The section then introduces the neural ODE, which parameterizes the time derivative of a state with a network and obtains the trajectory by numerical integration. Gradients come either through the solver steps or by the adjoint method, which integrates backward in time at the cost of additional integration.
sections.heading: Preliminaries
sections.headline: Direct-action policies output each action separately, while a neural ODE defines a field integrated over time.

sections.body: The method treats the action as the state of an ODE. A network $\mathbf{f}_{\theta}$ maps the current action, the proprioception, and an image-and-instruction embedding to the action velocity. At each decision step the embedding is held fixed, and a solver integrates the action over the chunk, starting from the last action. Training matches the integrated path to the demonstrated actions, so the field is never regressed against velocity labels. A contractive perturbation shifts the start point of a training segment and asks the path to return to the demonstration. A diversity head adds a sampled offset to the field to keep multi-modal behavior. In RL, the same field gives one Euler step per control step, and the gradient reaches early actions through the identity term.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: The method integrates a learned action field over each chunk, trains it on integrated paths, and adds a sampled diversity offset.

sections.body: The setup covers visuomotor imitation on LIBERO with zero-shot tests on LIBERO-plus, fine-tuning of pi0.5 and ImageWAM with the ODE head, a 2D navigation task with four routes, 14 real-robot tasks on four robots, and RL on SuperMimic for the 40 LAFAN1 clips with a simulated Unitree G1 humanoid. Baselines include six visuomotor policies that differ only in the action head, the original heads of pi0.5 and ImageWAM, and PPO in RL. The implementation uses H=8 steps integrated with RK4 and K=12 diversity components. Each visuomotor experiment repeats three random seeds. Real-robot methods train for 300 epochs, with 50 on the single-arm robot and 90 on the humanoid, and are evaluated with 20 trials. In RL, each actor trains for 3 hours on one GPU.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: The evaluation compares ODE policy with 14 baselines on simulated and real tasks, with shared backbones, data, and training schedules.

sections.body:
The section reports learning, execution, generalization, and multi-modality in simulation.
- **Learning:** After one epoch on LIBERO, ODE policy succeeds in 79.2% of episodes, nearly twice the best baseline. With 20 demonstrations per task it reaches 87.7% at epoch 100, above FM-DiT trained on all 50 (85.4%).
- **Large models:** In pi0.5 the ODE head reaches 96.0% after one epoch against 75.5%. In ImageWAM it reaches 82.6% against 24.6%.
- **Execution:** It generates a chunk of 8 actions in 5.7 ms, 10.8 times faster than FM-DiT, and has the lowest end-effector jerk at every checkpoint.
- **Generalization and modes:** On LIBERO-plus it leads after one epoch, 30.1% against 22.6% for ACT. On navigation its mode balance after one epoch is 3.9 times that of FM-DiT.
sections.heading: Simulation Results
sections.headline: In simulation, ODE policy learns faster, needs fewer demonstrations, generates actions faster, and keeps multiple behavior modes.

sections.body: The section reports four real robots. On the single-arm robot, trained for 50 epochs on 40 demonstrations per task, ODE policy succeeds in 15 and 14 of 20 trials on folding a sock and inserting a block, against 8 and 4 for the best baseline. On the dual-arm robot it reaches 60% on dahlia insertion against 40% for FM-DiT, and 75% on the microwave task against 20%. In the drawer task it uses both arm assignments. On the dexterous hand it places a can in 18 of 20 trials, against 14 for FM-DiT. On the humanoid it succeeds in 60% and 70% of trials against 35% and 30% for the original GR00T head. On three of the robots it generates chunks 3.5 to 27 times faster than the diffusion and flow baselines, even with RK4.
sections.heading: Real-World Results
sections.headline: On four real robots, ODE policy has the highest success rate on each reported task and transfers dexterous skills across labs.

sections.body: Each design choice is ablated with the others fixed. **Chunk length:** with H=1 the policy reaches only 76.4% at epoch 100 and is the slowest per action. From H=4 on, success stays above 91%, best at the default H=8. **Solver:** RK2 or Euler changes epoch-100 success by less than one point. **Contractive perturbation:** without it, one-epoch success drops from 79.8% to 58.4%, and the gap closes by epoch 20. **Seamless chunking:** restarting each chunk from the measured state lowers one-epoch success from 79.8% to 47.8% and gives a 3 to 4 times higher boundary ratio. **Proprioception:** the placements perform similarly from epoch 5. With K=4, the diversity head cannot reliably separate the four navigation routes.
sections.heading: Ablation Studies
sections.headline: Ablations show that chunking is essential and that removing the contractive perturbation drops the one-epoch success rate from 79.8% to 58.4%.

sections.body:
The discussion summarizes the results and sketches three preliminary extensions. On LIBERO, ODE policy reaches 79.2% after one epoch and 93.8% at epoch 100, and it matches FM-DiT with less than half the demonstrations. In RL, its return at the end of training is 0.885 against 0.845 for the direct-action actor.
- **Data without action labels:** feeding the field's velocity to the PD damping term raises Long success from 51% to 72%, but Spatial drops from 90% to 80%.
- **Arbitrary control rates:** changing the integration at deployment moves success from 94.8% to 92.8% with two substeps, and reaches 93.3% and 92.5% at 40 and 80 Hz.
- **Discrete signals:** integrating the binary gripper as a state gives 74.5% after one epoch, still above all baselines.
sections.heading: Discussion and Future Directions
sections.headline: Discussion argues continuity built into the policy improves efficiency across scales and suggests three preliminary extensions.

sections.body: The appendix gives the simulated benchmarks and the task settings of the single-arm, dual-arm, and dexterous-hand robots, with demonstration counts. It describes the humanoid setup through GR00T N1.7, where the vector field has about 5M parameters. It specifies the shared visuomotor encoder and training schedule, the ODE policy architecture, the sampling steps of each baseline, and the metrics, including RMS jerk and boundary ratio. Table S1 reports 8.82 ms per call with RK4 on one idle RTX 4090, which is 4.8 times less than FM-DiT. Further tables and figures cover LIBERO-plus perturbation types, navigation rollouts, RL returns, the diversity head at inference, and the vector field architecture.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists benchmark and robot details, training settings, timing tables, and extra generalization, multi-modal, and ablation results.
